problem: Mobile manipulation prior work uses disentangled modular skills for base, arm and perception (map, then plan, then act), causing compounding errors, delayed decisions, no whole-body coordination, and dependence on precise pre-built maps that fail in dynamic clutter.
motivation: Humans navigate clutter reactively with ego-centric vision, choosing where to look based on where they move and moving in order to see. A robot with a narrow-FoV actuated camera must couple camera control, base and arm motion, but RL from rendered depth is too slow (about 61x slower than scandots).
key_idea: Train a single end-to-end RL policy that jointly outputs base, arm and camera actions using only field-of-view-visible privileged scandots, then distill it via DAgger into an ego-depth student, so the robot learns to move to see and see to move without maps.
insight: Restricting privileged teacher information to what the camera could actually see forces the teacher to learn useful camera behavior that is distillable to depth. Ablations show active vision matters (FixCam gets 0.20-0.26 hard-scenario success vs about 0.9+ for SPIN), and PointNet permutation invariance helps (NoPointNet 0.57-0.63 hard). Decoupled (DVO) and coupled (CVO) optimization perform similarly, so DVO is an easier optimization path. Limiting visibility range to 2m or less works better than 5m (0.86 SR, 1.21m distance to goal).
method: Phase 1 teacher RL (scandots): PPO with BPTT trains LSTM (256) navigation and pick policies in IsaacGym on procedural corridors; obstacles are given as bounding-box xyz scandots encoded by PointNet (16-d latent), and only scandots inside the camera FoV are provided (masking function F).
Coupled Visuomotor Optimization (CVO): a single RL policy sees proprioception plus visible scandots and outputs robot and camera actions jointly; it needs billions of samples.

Decoupled Visuomotor Optimization (DVO): phase 1a learns navigation with all local scandots; phase 1b trains a partially observed policy, initialized from 1a, to output camera and robot actions while matching 1a robot actions.

Pick policy: LSTM given proprioception, initial object location and FoV-masked current object location; reward combines reach distance, grasp contact (>10N) and lift; the nav policy switches to the pick policy near the object.

Phase 2 depth distillation: a CNN (3 conv + 3 FC, 58x87 depth) replaces scandots latents and is trained with L2 loss to the teacher's actions using asynchronous DAgger (2.5x speedup); for the real robot, hole-filling and temporal depth filtering, and YOLO plus depth deprojection give the object goal.

Rewards: nav reward is distance to goal plus forward progress (0.1 each); the pick reward is 0.5 for reach and 0.5 for lift, with a joint velocity penalty (-0.03) for smoothness and sim2real transfer.

setting.backbone: LSTM policy (256 hidden) + PointNet teacher, distilled into depth-CNN + LSTM student (trained from scratch, RL + DAgger)
setting.training_data: Procedurally generated corridors with obstacles and tables in IsaacGymEnvs (8192 envs; 6h phase 1 + 10h phase 2 on an RTX 3090); no real or web data
setting.observation: Ego-centric depth image (58x87) from actuated head camera (87° x 58° FoV) + proprioception (joint positions/velocities, end-effector position) + goal position
setting.action_space: Continuous: base linear/angular velocity, position targets for arm, wrist, gripper and 2-DoF camera at 10Hz
setting.privileged: none at test time (scandots and object location used only in the teacher; the student uses depth; goal position is given; the FixCam and Mapping baselines differ)

numbers_note: Custom simulation benchmarks, not standard navigation benchmarks; only hard-difficulty results for the two main variants are listed (easy and medium are near 1.00 in Table 1). Real-world tables have a small number of trials.
results: SPIN (CVO/DVO) reaches 0.90-0.96 success on hard cluttered simulation scenarios, versus FixCam 0.16-0.26 and NoPointNet 0.57-0.63, and roughly matches the Mapping baseline (which has noisy privileged map info). In the real world it beats a lidar gmapping/move_base classical baseline by 20-40% on static obstacles and 0.6 vs 0.0-0.2 on dynamic obstacles, showing emergent avoidance without dynamic-obstacle training.
limitations: Relies on stereo depth, so it collides with glass or shiny surfaces; RGB perception is left as future work.
Short-range local reactive navigation only (visibility of 2m or less, goals within about 5m), with no global memory or planning.
Real-world evaluation is small-scale (few trials, two scenes) and the classical baseline uses only 2D lidar and cannot handle floating obstacles.
